planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; KSU-Atwood needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar such as Sunflower or Susquehanna nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.

directions: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first year or two before they can handle full sun. KSU-Atwood is a Kentucky State University research program release bred from Atwood x Overleese parentage, chosen for consistently large, well-filled fruit with rich, sweet flesh and a relatively low seed count for the species. Trees are vigorous and productive once established, ripening their crop in the midseason window and holding fruit quality well compared to many wild seedling trees. Because pawpaws are not self-fertile, interplant with a second unrelated cultivar within about 50 feet and consider hand-pollinating with a small paintbrush during the brief, unpleasant-smelling maroon bloom, since the flies and beetles that pollinate pawpaw in the wild are often scarce in home gardens.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Prima 1216 needs a second, unrelated pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and dependable fruit set.

directions: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil, shading young trees for their first couple of seasons before exposing them to full sun. Prima 1216 is one of the oldest named pawpaw selections still in commerce, originally chosen from wild Michigan trees by pawpaw breeder Corwin Davis decades before the modern named-cultivar boom, and it remains valued for early, reliable ripening and consistent, medium-sized fruit with mild, smooth-textured flesh. It tends to bear at a younger age than many other named selections, making it a good anchor tree for a new pawpaw patch. Interplant with a genetically distinct cultivar such as Sunflower or Wabash for cross-pollination, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during bloom if fruit set seems light in early years.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Taytwo needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.

directions: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving toward full sun once established. Taytwo is a historic Ohio-origin pawpaw selection long grown for its heavy, dependable production and medium-sized fruit with good, smooth-textured flavor, and it remains one of the most widely planted older cultivars for home orchards because it crops reliably even in cooler seasons. Vigorous, cold-hardy trees form the classic pyramidal pawpaw shape and tolerate the deep shade of establishment years better than most fruit trees, though full sun once mature produces the heaviest crops. Because pawpaws will not self-pollinate, plant a second unrelated cultivar such as Sunflower or Susquehanna nearby and hand-pollinate with a small brush during the maroon spring bloom for the most consistent fruit set.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Sweet Alice needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.

directions: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving them toward full sun as they mature. Sweet Alice is a historic Indiana-origin pawpaw prized for exceptionally large, sweet fruit with a mild, low-astringency flavor that many tasters rank among the best of the older named selections, though it can bear somewhat irregularly compared to more modern, heavier-cropping cultivars. Trees are vigorous with the typical pyramidal pawpaw habit and glossy drooping foliage, and they tolerate the wet-but-drained bottomland soils pawpaw favors in the wild. Because pawpaws require cross-pollination, plant Sweet Alice with a genetically unrelated cultivar such as Shenandoah or Wabash, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during bloom to improve fruit set in home settings where natural pollinators are scarce.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Zimmerman needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.

directions: Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving toward full sun once established. Zimmerman is an Ohio-origin pawpaw selection known for very sweet, richly flavored flesh with a notably low seed count for the species, making the fruit easier to eat fresh than many wild seedlings. It ripens in the midseason window and produces medium to large fruit on a vigorous, cold-hardy tree with the classic pyramidal pawpaw form and large, tropical-looking drooping leaves. Because pawpaws will not set fruit from their own pollen, interplant Zimmerman with an unrelated cultivar such as Susquehanna or Taytwo, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief spring bloom to improve fruit set in home orchard settings.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program
